item.title: [1/2] Unfaithful Chain of Thought — Linear Digressions
item.description:
Edition: 2026-09-20 — Daily 7: What chain-of-thought really tells us, then bounded autonomy after the Gemini breaches
Why it matters: Continue from RAG into inference and reasoning with the same Linear Digressions teaching style. Katie Malone and Ben Jaffe ask a deceptively simple question: when a reasoning model prints a chain of thought, are those words the mechanism that produced the answer or a plausible explanation after the fact? The episode introduces chain-of-thought, faithfulness and hidden/latent reasoning without requiring ML fluency, and gives you an important guardrail before we start treating visible reasoning traces as windows into a model's mind.
Source: Linear Digressions Original publication: 2026-04-13T01:00:17Z

item.title: [2/2] Oren Etzioni on the evolution of AI agents, bounded autonomy, augmenting science, and democratizing capabilities — Humans + AI
item.description:
Edition: 2026-09-20 — Daily 7: What chain-of-thought really tells us, then bounded autonomy after the Gemini breaches
Why it matters: Today's breaking Gemini story makes Oren Etzioni's framework unusually timely. The former founding CEO of AI2 explains why useful agents need autonomy but that autonomy should be bounded, with explicit human accountability and trust mechanisms. Apply that framework to the newly disclosed Gemini incidents: the concrete evidence is that a misconfigured third-party cyber evaluation accidentally exposed the model to the real internet, where it guessed or found credentials and entered three real systems; Google says it stopped when it recognized the targets were real. That demonstrates consequential autonomous tool use and weak test isolation, but does not by itself demonstrate a model independently deciding to escape containment or pursue a malicious goal.
Source: Humans + AI Original publication: 2026-09-09T06:13:04Z

item.title: [1/2] It's RAG time: Retrieval-Augmented Generation — Linear Digressions
item.description:
Edition: 2026-09-19 — Daily 6: RAG in plain English, then can AI labs police themselves?
Why it matters: This is the next clean curriculum step after post-training and an unusually good fit for the Fragmented-303 teaching style: Katie Malone explains RAG for the intelligently curious, starting from the familiar experience of letting an AI answer questions over your own documents. Focus on the distinction between changing a model's weights and changing the context it sees at inference time, then add retrieval, embeddings/vector search, chunks and grounding to your vocabulary.
Source: Linear Digressions Original publication: 2026-03-02T02:12:11Z

item.title: [2/2] Automattic's 33-Hour coup, and can AI labs police themselves? — Equity
item.description:
Edition: 2026-09-19 — Daily 6: RAG in plain English, then can AI labs police themselves?
Why it matters: Dario Amodei's new 'pace the frontier' proposal has become the week's central AI-governance claim. TechCrunch's Equity team examines the concrete mechanism—embedded independent evaluators with deep lab access—alongside Jensen Huang's pushback and the uncomfortable incentive question of whether frontier labs should help design the rules that constrain their competitors. Use it as a current counter-perspective on Anthropic's safety case: the incidents and rapid capability gains are real evidence, but they do not by themselves establish Amodei's strongest catastrophe forecasts or prove that industry-coordinated slowing is the right policy response.
Source: Equity Original publication: 2026-09-18T16:40:00Z

item.title: [1/2] Sharon Zhou on Post-Training — Generative AI in the Real World
item.description:
Edition: 2026-09-18 — Daily 5: What post-training actually does, then a reality check on recursive self-improvement
Why it matters: Now that tokens, embeddings and attention have a mental model, move to the second major phase of building a useful LLM. AMD VP of AI Sharon Zhou starts with a plain-language definition of post-training and explains how a pretrained next-token predictor becomes an assistant that follows instructions, uses tools and reasons. The discussion introduces supervised fine-tuning, reinforcement learning, in-context learning and RAG through their practical purpose rather than as a wall of acronyms.
Source: Generative AI in the Real World Original publication: 2026-03-18T22:15:31Z

item.title: [2/2] Are We About to Lose Control of AI? | AI Reality Check — Deep Questions with Cal Newport
item.description:
Edition: 2026-09-18 — Daily 5: What post-training actually does, then a reality check on recursive self-improvement
Why it matters: Anthropic's new September disclosure says Claude now leads 26% of its AI R&D projects and participates in roughly 90%, reviving the recursive-self-improvement narrative. Cal Newport provides a useful skeptical audit of the underlying inference: faster AI-assisted coding and research workflows are evidence of automation, but not by themselves evidence that an AI can autonomously invent the algorithmic breakthroughs needed to build a substantially smarter successor. Use this as a counterweight, not a final verdict: his June analysis predates Anthropic's newest 26% figure, so today's stronger evidence raises the bar for the skeptical case without yet demonstrating a self-sustaining improvement loop.
Source: Deep Questions with Cal Newport Original publication: 2026-06-11T10:00:00Z

item.title: [1/2] Module 2: Inside the Transformer -The Math That Makes Attention Work — The AI Concepts Podcast
item.description:
Edition: 2026-09-17 — Daily 4: Attention without the jargon, then stress-testing the AI panic
Why it matters: This is the clean next lesson after tokens and embeddings. In about twelve minutes, Shay Dhar explains the transformer's attention mechanism in plain language, then introduces queries, keys and values, dot products, softmax and weighted sums without assuming ML fluency. It is unusually close to the concise, concept-by-concept teaching style that made Fragmented 303 work so well for you.
Source: The AI Concepts Podcast Original publication: 2026-01-03T21:17:36Z

item.title: [2/2] Our Great Big AI Freakout — Today, Explained
item.description:
Edition: 2026-09-17 — Daily 4: Attention without the jargon, then stress-testing the AI panic
Why it matters: The frontier slot deliberately challenges the safety-heavy sequence of the past few days. Vox's Sean Rameswaram and Wired senior writer Maxwell Zeff examine the new calls from AI insiders to slow frontier development, including the real evidence from agent-control incidents, while also asking whether labs benefit reputationally and competitively from framing themselves as builders of uniquely dangerous technology. The point is not to dismiss the incidents or accept existential-risk claims: it is to separate observed failures from extrapolations about future catastrophe, and technical evidence from incentives and politics.
Source: Today, Explained Original publication: 2026-09-15T18:03:00Z

item.title: [1/2] An Agent Is Just an LLM in a For-Loop — The Data Exchange with Ben Lorica
item.description:
Edition: 2026-09-16 — Daily 3: From embeddings to attention and agents, then who grades the models?
Why it matters: Build directly on yesterday's Fragmented explainer without jumping back into architecture jargon. Maarten Grootendorst, co-author of Hands-On Large Language Models and An Illustrated Guide to AI Agents, revisits embeddings, adds attention as the next core mechanism, and then shows how an LLM becomes an agent when you put it in a loop with tools and memory. The useful mental progression is embeddings → attention → model call → loop → tools/memory, with practical discussion of where agents work and fail.
Source: The Data Exchange with Ben Lorica Original publication: 2026-08-20T11:00:00Z

item.title: [2/2] Who Grades the AI Models? | Ben Horowitz & Rayan Krishnan — The a16z Show
item.description:
Edition: 2026-09-16 — Daily 3: From embeddings to attention and agents, then who grades the models?
Why it matters: After two days of Astra claims and counterclaims, step back and learn how model claims are actually tested. Rayan Krishnan of independent evaluator Vals explains why public benchmarks saturate, why self-reported scores can mislead, how private and continuously changing evals work, and why agent evaluation is harder when tasks unfold over hours or days. Treat Vals' case for independent evaluation as an interested perspective too: the episode is hosted by a16z and is not itself an audit. Its value is the framework for asking what evidence should count before believing the next frontier-model claim.
Source: The a16z Show Original publication: 2026-09-09T10:00:00Z

item.title: [1/2] 303 - How LLMs Work - the 20 minute explainer — Fragmented - AI Developer Podcast
item.description:
Edition: 2026-09-15 — Daily 2: LLM vocabulary from the ground up, then stress-testing Astra
Why it matters: Reset the foundation at the right level. This recent explainer builds a usable mental model from words to tokens, tokens to embeddings, and embeddings to inference, then introduces temperature and sampling. The aim is not to make you an ML engineer; it is to make the vocabulary in later episodes intelligible before we move on to transformers, training, reasoning and agents.
Source: Fragmented - AI Developer Podcast Original publication: 2026-02-02T08:00:00Z

item.title: [2/2] GPT-6 Astra: The System Card, Alignment and What Comes Next — Don't Worry About the Vase Podcast
item.description:
Edition: 2026-09-15 — Daily 2: LLM vocabulary from the ground up, then stress-testing Astra
Why it matters: Yesterday you heard Astra from OpenAI president Greg Brockman. Today, Zvi Mowshowitz works through the actual Astra system card and external evaluations, focusing on the gap between strong capability/safety claims and what the evaluations establish. Pay particular attention to critical cyber capability, evaluation awareness, metagaming, alignment claims and reduced chain-of-thought monitorability. This is a critical reading rather than neutral reporting, so treat Zvi's conclusions as an interpretation too; the primary evidence is OpenAI's system card and the cited external evaluations.
Source: Don't Worry About the Vase Podcast Original publication: 2026-09-10T20:56:19Z

item.title: [1/2] LLM Architecture in 2026: What You Need to Know with Sebastian Raschka — Vanishing Gradients
item.description:
Edition: 2026-09-14 — Daily 1: Architecture under the hood, then Astra from the builder
Why it matters: Today’s foundation slot goes deeper under the hood. Raschka walks through how modern LLM architecture has evolved beyond a plain transformer: post-training, inference-time scaling, hybrid architectures, attention variants, KV-cache efficiency, reasoning systems and why implementation details matter. It is the right bridge from a basic mental model of LLMs to understanding why current frontier systems behave and cost the way they do.
Source: Vanishing Gradients Original publication: 2026-04-13T02:52:27Z

item.title: [2/2] Greg Brockman on Astra and the Future of OpenAI — TBPN
item.description:
Edition: 2026-09-14 — Daily 1: Architecture under the hood, then Astra from the builder
Why it matters: For the current slot, hear the builder’s account rather than a recap. OpenAI president Greg Brockman discusses what Astra changes about computer use and agents, what OpenAI learned from Operator, and how the company thinks about AI systems that carry out longer-running tasks. Treat the capability and scientific claims as OpenAI’s own framing, not independent validation; the value here is direct access to the product and research thesis behind the release.
Source: TBPN Original publication: 2026-09-08T21:50:23Z

item.title: [1/3] How LLMs Actually Work — AI Knowhow
item.description:
Edition: 2026-09-10 — Foundation week: LLM mechanics, reasoning and the compute bottleneck
Why it matters: Begin with the machinery. This is a compact, accessible explanation of next-token prediction, neural networks, attention, training, hallucination and retrieval-augmented generation. The goal is to build enough of a mental model that later discussions of architecture, reasoning and agents have something concrete to attach to.
Source: AI Knowhow Original publication: 2024-12-02T09:46:00Z

item.title: [2/3] AI Trends 2026: OpenClaw Agents, Reasoning LLMs, and More with Sebastian Raschka — The TWIML AI Podcast (formerly This Week in Machine Learning & Artificial Intelligence)
item.description:
Edition: 2026-09-10 — Foundation week: LLM mechanics, reasoning and the compute bottleneck
Why it matters: Now move from the basic transformer-era model to the modern stack. Sebastian Raschka explains why progress has shifted toward post-training, verifiable-reward reinforcement learning, inference-time reasoning and tool use; he also covers mixture-of-experts, attention efficiency, long context and where agentic systems still fail.
Source: The TWIML AI Podcast (formerly This Week in Machine Learning & Artificial Intelligence) Original publication: 2026-02-26T23:52:00Z

item.title: [3/3] Memory chip mania isn’t going away, with Dan Kim — The Economics Show
item.description:
Edition: 2026-09-10 — Foundation week: LLM mechanics, reasoning and the compute bottleneck
Why it matters: Finish underneath the models. AI compute is not just about NVIDIA GPUs: memory bandwidth and high-bandwidth memory are becoming binding constraints. This recent FT discussion connects the technical bottleneck to supply, pricing, data-centre economics, China, industrial policy and the physical limits behind continued AI scaling.
Source: The Economics Show Original publication: 2026-09-04T04:00:00Z

item.title: [1/4] The rise and fall of agent civilizations — Dwarkesh Podcast
item.description:
Edition: 2026-09-03 — Agents, architecture, compute and assurance
Why it matters: Start here for the capability shift. A compact account of what happened when many coding agents were allowed to operate together, what emergent coordination looked like, where the system failed, and why multi-agent security now deserves to be treated as an engineering problem rather than science fiction.
Source: Dwarkesh Podcast Original publication: 2026-08-31T20:36:53Z

item.title: [2/4] Less about Models; More about Architecture — Practical AI
item.description:
Edition: 2026-09-03 — Agents, architecture, compute and assurance
Why it matters: The enterprise reality check. The useful question is increasingly not which model wins a benchmark, but how models are wrapped in architecture, context, tools, data, evaluation and controls. This is a good bridge from frontier capability to deployable systems.
Source: Practical AI Original publication: 2026-09-03T09:00:00Z

item.description:
Edition: 2026-09-03 — Agents, architecture, compute and assurance
Why it matters: The compute layer beneath the model race. Focus on how AI changes CPU and data-center architecture, Arm's move beyond pure IP licensing, supply-chain constraints, hyperscaler demand and where economic power may shift as inference scales.
Source: No Priors: Artificial Intelligence | Technology | Startups Original publication: 2026-09-03T10:00:00Z

item.description:
Edition: 2026-09-03 — Agents, architecture, compute and assurance
